newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark slides by US close but Dow cushions fall.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark slides by US close but Dow cushions fall.

text.p: Dollar/mark fell sharply after surprisingly weak U.S. manufacturing and wage data diminished prospects for a near-term interest rate hike, but a furious rally in U.S. asset markets sparked a dollar recovery in late trade, dealers said on Tuesday.

Investors who had hoped to capitalize on a rising gap in interest rates between the United States and Germany began to sell dollars after the U.S. Labor Department reported the first quarter employment cost index rose only 0.6 percent, below Wall Street forecasts for a 0.9 percent rise.
A Commerce Department release one hour later, reporting that March U.S. durable good orders fell more than expected, heightened dollar sales, traders said.
"People have been trading the interest rate differentials for quite a while now and today would be a sell day," said Russell LaScala, chief dealer at Citibank.
March durable goods dropped 3.0 percent, the largest drop since August 1996 and well below Wall Street expectations for a flat reading.
However, dollar/yen stood nearly unchanged for most of the session as dealers focused on buying marks for yen.
The dollar made a small recovery in late U.S. trade, buoyed by a furious rally in U.S. asset markets instigated by the soft economic data.

The Dow Jones industrials index rose 179 points to close at 6,962 while by late trade the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond had gained 1-18/32 points to yield 6.98 percent, its first dip below the 7.00 percent level since March 26.

Also underpinning the U.S. unit was high expectations for first quarter gross domestic product growth and employment data due later this week and a benign outcome from last weekend's meeting between the Group of Seven in Washington.
"The trend higher is still intact. There seems to be a little bit of a correction, but we could see 1.74 (marks) by later this week," LaScala said.

The dollar rose to a 55-month high of 1.7389 marks and fell just shy of its 37-month peak at 127.16 yen on Monday after the G7 issued a statement which barely differed from that issued at the last G7 summit in February, which also failed to halt the appreciation of the dollar.
Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has risen more than 12 percent against the mark and almost 10 percent against the yen.
"People seem to have spent most of the day buying marks and selling yen," said Tom Arnold, chief dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
"What we saw today was some good fund profit-taking on the dollar, selling the dollar and buying marks the whole way down starting at around 1.7315," he added.

The dollar fell nearly a pfennig at its low and closed at 1.7240/50 on Tuesday from 1.7320/30 at the U.S. open. Against the yen, the dollar inched higher just before the close to end at 126.89/94 yen compared to 126.80/85 at the open.
A host of comments from German and U.S. officals had little effect on dollar trade as they did not significantly differ from the stance taken at the G7 meeting, traders said.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday that German policymakers were united in their view of not wanting a much stronger dollar. This complimented Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's remark on Monday that the United States is interested in a strong, but not stronger, dollar.
Waigel also said that the G7 statement last weekend sent a signal to the currency markets and now Germany will "wait and see".
Bundesbank directorate member Helmut Schieber also said that foreign exchange rates will be watched carefully.

In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4675/85 Swiss francs from 1.4740/50 and Canadian $1.3974/79 from C$1.4006/11. Sterling rose to $1.6318/28 from 1.6218/28. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7823/28 from $0.7795/00.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
